footer_note: ROSE Therapeutic Farm, Monthly Scorecard, Sept 2026
headline: We took the account over on May 19. Every day since then through the end of August, ad spend went from $8,270 to $21,046 and attributed sales went from $48,997 to $110,316, up 125%. Bookings rose 90%, from 532 to 1013. ROAS moved from 5.9x to 5.2x, which is what happens when you scale spend into colder audiences, and that period still includes August, when ads were paused most of the month at your request.
chart_lead: Attributed sales since takeover, each period against the exact same dates last year. August is low by design, ads were paused most of the month at your request.
roas_note: ROAS is a ratio, not revenue. At low spend, ads reach only your warmest audience, so the ratio looks high while the dollars stay small. Scaling reaches colder audiences: the ratio comes down and the total goes up. Last year, $8,270 at 5.9x produced $48,997. This year, $21,046 at 5.2x produced $110,316. Average booking value rose too, from $92 to $109, up 18%. And the FareHarbor checkout means some bookings never reach Meta, so over any full season these figures are a floor, not a ceiling.
roas_note_jared_alt: ROAS is a ratio, not revenue. When spend is small, ads only reach the warmest audiences, so the ratio looks high but the total dollars stay small. Scaling spend reaches colder audiences, which lowers the ratio and raises the total. Last year this account spent $8,270 at 5.9x and produced $48,997. This year it spent $21,046 at 5.2x and produced $110,316. These numbers are also undercounted: Meta cannot see walk-ins, phone bookings, or every FareHarbor checkout, so the true return is higher. Average booking value grew from $92 to $109, up 18%.

revcompare.title: What Meta reports, and what actually landed
revcompare.lead: Meta only counts a booking when it can follow the guest all the way through the FareHarbor checkout. Your FareHarbor totals include everything: repeat guests, walk-ins, phone bookings and organic. Every month where both numbers exist is shown below, full calendar months on both sides.
revcompare.why: They measure different things. Meta records a sale on the day someone clicks or views an ad, and counts it even when that guest is a repeat visitor or a referral who might have booked anyway. It also misses people who saw an ad and later booked by phone or after a Google search. FareHarbor records every booking, on the day it is made. So Meta's figure is the platform's own estimate, and the FareHarbor total is what actually landed.
